Retain option (a): Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project — specifically connects Mizoram to Sittwe port via the Kaladan River, supporting India's Act East Policy.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication-adjacent trap uses the Stilwell Road (option c) — a real, historically significant India–Myanmar–China route that sounds like it could be the answer for an 'Act East Policy connectivity' question. Students who do not specifically recall the Kaladan project may default to Stilwell Road, which is genuinely associated with NE India–Myanmar connectivity.
solution.final_explanation:
India's Act East Policy prioritises connectivity with Southeast Asia through the northeastern states. The project in question is the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project.

• Option (a): Correct — the Kaladan project creates a multimodal route connecting Mizoram to Myanmar's Sittwe port via the Kaladan River and overland road, providing India's landlocked northeast a new trade outlet.
• Option (b): The India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway connects Moreh (Manipur) to Mae Sot (Thailand) — a different project entirely.
• Option (c): The Stilwell Road (Ledo Road) is a WWII Allied supply route from Assam through Myanmar to China — it has historical significance but is not the 'Act East' project described.
• Option (d): The BCIM Economic Corridor is a broader multilateral framework linking Bangladesh, China, India, and Myanmar — distinct from the Kaladan project.

Value Addition:
• Sittwe port in Rakhine State (Myanmar) is the western terminus of the Kaladan project; goods move by sea from Kolkata to Sittwe, then by river/road to Mizoram.
• India's 2023 decision to review the Free Movement Regime with Myanmar has implications for cross-border project implementation.
• The Kaladan project reduces India's dependence on the Siliguri Corridor for NE connectivity.

solution.concept_anchor: China rejects McMahon Line — does not accept Arunachal as Indian
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a tempts students who know both facts — China rejects the McMahon Line AND claims Arunachal — and assume R directly causes A (i.e., the non-acceptance of the line is why China claims Arunachal). This confuses correlation with causation.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is A correct? — China does claim Arunachal Pradesh as 'South Tibet (Zangnan),' issuing 'standardised' Chinese names for places within it and objecting to Indian leaders visiting the state. A is factually correct.
Step 2: Is R correct? — China has consistently maintained it did not ratify the Simla Convention (1914) and considers the McMahon Line illegal. R is factually correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — China's rejection of the McMahon Line is the underlying legal basis for its Arunachal claim — R does causally explain why China claims Arunachal: because China doesn't accept the boundary line that places Arunachal in India. R correctly explains A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A → correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: In this case, unusually, R does correctly explain A — China's rejection of the McMahon Line (R) is the direct legal foundation of its claim over Arunachal Pradesh (A). The trap is the reverse: a student trained to suspect causal relationships in A-R questions may over-apply scepticism and choose (b) when (a) is actually correct. The strong distractor is option (b), not option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Assertion (A): China actively contests India's sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh, calling it 'South Tibet' (Zangnan), issuing Chinese place names for towns within it, and objecting to visits by Indian leaders. A is factually correct.

Reason (R): China's non-acceptance of the Simla Convention (1914) and the McMahon Line it produced is China's longstanding legal position. R is factually correct.

Causal link: Does R explain A? Yes — directly. China's entire legal argument for claiming Arunachal Pradesh rests on its rejection of the McMahon Line. If the line is illegitimate (China's view), the territory south of it (including Arunachal) cannot be Indian. R is the legal foundation of A.

Both correct, R explains A → Option (a).

Value Addition:
• China has issued 'standardised' Chinese names for places in Arunachal Pradesh in 2017, 2021, and 2023 — a pattern of asserting nominal sovereignty.
• The 6th Dalai Lama was born in Tawang — adding religious-cultural weight to China's Arunachal claim.
• India responds by calling Arunachal Pradesh an 'integral and inalienable part of India.'

solution.concept_anchor: Demarcated vs delimited vs undemarcated boundaries

statement_analysis.statement: A 'demarcated' boundary is one that has been physically marked on the ground with pillars, fences, or other markers, while a 'delimited' boundary is one that has been defined only on maps and in treaty documents.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard legal-geographic distinction: delimitation is map-based; demarcation is physical ground-marking. Both are required for a fully formalised boundary.

statement_analysis.statement: The Line of Actual Control (LAC) between India and China is delimited but not yet demarcated.
statement_analysis.reason: The LAC is neither delimited nor demarcated — both sides have different perceptions of where it runs, so it has not even been agreed upon on a map (delimited), let alone marked on the ground (demarcated).

statement_analysis.statement: The India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement (2015) involved the exchange of enclaves and required a constitutional amendment because it involved transfers of territory.
statement_analysis.reason: The LBA required the 100th Amendment Act (2015) because exchanging enclaves meant India both ceded and acquired territory, which under Article 368 required a constitutional amendment.

statement_analysis.statement: India and Bangladesh jointly maintain boundary pillars along their shared border through a Joint Boundary Working Group.
statement_analysis.reason: India and Bangladesh have established joint border management mechanisms, including working groups that maintain boundary pillars along the ~4,156 km shared border.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all four correct) traps students who verify Statements 1, 3, and 4 correctly but fail to catch that Statement 2 incorrectly says the LAC is 'delimited' — the LAC is not even delimited.
elimination_logic: Verify Pair 1: Demarcated = on-ground markers; delimited = map/treaty only — standard geographic distinction. Correct.
Verify Pair 2: The LAC is often described as 'not demarcated' but the full truth is it is not even delimited — no agreed map exists. Calling it 'delimited but not demarcated' is incorrect.
Verify Pair 3: LBA 2015 required 100th Amendment Act — correct; territorial transfers need constitutional amendment. Correct.
Verify Pair 4: India–Bangladesh Joint Boundary Working Group for pillar maintenance — correct. Correct.
Three pairs (1, 3, 4) are correct; Pair 2 is incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2: students who know 'LAC is not demarcated' often stop there and accept 'delimited but not demarcated' as a reasonable partial description. In fact, the LAC is neither — there is no agreed map between India and China showing where the LAC runs. The absence of delimitation (not just demarcation) is the precise and critical distinction that elevates this question above surface knowledge.
solution.final_explanation:
The legal status of international boundaries — whether demarcated, delimited, or neither — has significant strategic and diplomatic implications.

• Pair 1 — Correct: Delimitation = treaty/map level; demarcation = physical on-ground markers. A boundary can be delimited but not demarcated (common in remote areas), or in rare cases neither.
• Pair 2 — Incorrect: The LAC with China is neither delimited nor demarcated. India and China do not agree on where the LAC runs — there is no mutually accepted map. Describing it as 'delimited but not demarcated' overstates the level of agreement.
• Pair 3 — Correct: The 100th Amendment Act enabled the LBA by authorising the territorial exchange with Bangladesh.
• Pair 4 — Correct: India–Bangladesh border management includes joint working groups and joint pillar inspection — a sign of the more cooperative, demarcated nature of this boundary.

Value Addition:
• The LoC with Pakistan is demarcated (following Simla Agreement 1972) — a critical contrast with the LAC.
• India's border with Nepal and Bhutan is largely demarcated through bilateral surveys.
• Border pillars are maintained at fixed intervals; any damage or displacement becomes a diplomatic incident.

solution.concept_anchor: Palk Strait vs Palk Bay vs Gulf of Mannar — geographic distinctions
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (Palk Bay) is the strong distractor because students who know the Palk region may confuse Palk Bay with Palk Strait — both are in the same geographic area — and fail to notice that Adam's Bridge, not Palk Bay, is the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: geographic features that separate or lie between India and Sri Lanka in the relevant water bodies.
Palk Strait — the narrow water body (~65 km) separating India from Sri Lanka at its narrowest. Belongs to the India–Sri Lanka separation geography.
Palk Bay — the body of water east of the Palk Strait, enclosed between India's southeastern coast and Sri Lanka's northwestern coast. Belongs to the same geographic area.
Gulf of Mannar — the body of water south of Adam's Bridge, between India (Tamil Nadu) and Sri Lanka. Belongs to the India–Sri Lanka maritime area.

Adam's Bridge (Ram Setu) — a chain of natural limestone shoals connecting India to Sri Lanka. It is a physical geographic feature, not a water body. The other three are water bodies. Adam's Bridge is the odd one out.
Select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap: Palk Strait and Palk Bay share the 'Palk' name and are geographically adjacent, making students confuse them and potentially mark Palk Bay as the odd one out. The true odd one out is Adam's Bridge — a submerged limestone ridge, not a water body — but students fixated on the Palk/Gulf categorisation may miss this structural difference.
solution.final_explanation:
The geographic features surrounding the India–Sri Lanka maritime zone are a recurring UPSC topic. Three of the four options are water bodies; one is not.

• Option (a) — Palk Strait: A narrow water channel (~65 km at its narrowest) separating the Indian mainland from Sri Lanka's northwest coast. It is a water body.
• Option (b) — Palk Bay: A semi-enclosed sea area east of the Palk Strait, between India's southeastern coast and Sri Lanka. It is a water body.
• Option (c) — Gulf of Mannar: A body of water south of Adam's Bridge, between Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka's western coast. It is a water body.
• Option (d) — Adam's Bridge (Ram Setu): A chain of natural limestone shoals and sandbanks connecting Rameswaram (India) to Mannar (Sri Lanka). It is a physical geographic structure, not a water body — the odd one out.

Value Addition:
• Katchatheevu island is in the Palk Strait — it was ceded to Sri Lanka in 1974.
• The Sethusamudram Canal Project proposes dredging through Adam's Bridge to create a navigable channel.
• Adam's Bridge sits at approximately 1 metre below sea level in places, surfacing during low tides.

solution.concept_anchor: Bhutan — only neighbour without maritime boundary

statement_analysis.statement: Among all of India's neighbours, Bhutan is the only country that shares neither a maritime boundary nor a sea coastline with India.
statement_analysis.reason: Bhutan is a landlocked country with no coastline — it shares only a land boundary with India and has no maritime interface with India whatsoever. All other land neighbours (Pakistan, China, Bangladesh, Myanmar) either share maritime boundaries with India or have their own coastlines.

statement_analysis.statement: Nepal's open border with India allows unrestricted movement of people but restricts the movement of goods to designated trade points only.
statement_analysis.reason: The open border policy between India and Nepal (rooted in the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship) allows relatively free movement of both people and goods — there is no restriction of goods to designated points only in the way the statement implies; goods cross at multiple points.

statement_analysis.statement: The Sugauli Treaty (1816) established the Kali (Mahakali) River as the western boundary between Nepal and British India, which remains the basis of the modern India–Nepal western boundary.
statement_analysis.reason: The Sugauli Treaty used the Kali/Mahakali River to demarcate the western boundary; this remains the accepted reference for the modern India–Nepal western boundary, with the source of the Kali being the disputed point in the Kalapani issue.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) tempts students who know Statements 1 and 3 are correct and may accept Statement 2 as a reasonable-sounding restriction they haven't specifically memorised.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Bhutan is indeed landlocked with no maritime interface. No other land neighbour is in this position — China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Myanmar all have coastlines. Statement 1 is correct.

Check Statement 2: The India–Nepal open border policy allows movement of people AND goods with minimal restrictions — not restricted goods to designated points only. Statement 2 is incorrect (overstated restriction).
Check Statement 3: The Sugauli Treaty (1816) using the Kali River as the western boundary is an established historical fact. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in Statement 2 adds the qualifier 'restricts the movement of goods to designated trade points only' — a plausible-sounding restriction that does not accurately describe the open border. The 1950 treaty enables relatively free movement of both people and goods. Students unfamiliar with the precise terms of the Nepal open border may accept this restriction as real.
solution.final_explanation:
India's relationship with Nepal and Bhutan are both close but structurally different.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Bhutan is the only Indian neighbour that shares no maritime boundary and has no coastline. It is entirely landlocked and has only a land boundary with India (and with China). This is a key UPSC-relevant fact.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The India–Nepal open border under the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship allows relatively free movement of both people and goods — both citizens and traders cross at multiple points without visa requirements. The 'designated trade points only' restriction is an overstatement that misrepresents the policy.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Sugauli Treaty (1816) used the Kali/Mahakali River as the western boundary; this treaty remains the legal foundation of the modern India–Nepal western boundary.

Value Addition:
• Security concerns around the open Nepal border include cross-border crime, counterfeit currency movement, and potential infiltration — used in arguments for border management reform.
• Bhutan's 2007 Friendship Treaty gave it more independent foreign policy space while retaining close coordination with India.
• The Gandak and Kosi river agreements with Nepal are separate bilateral arrangements governing water sharing and flood management.

solution.concept_anchor: Indus Waters Treaty allocation — eastern vs western rivers
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a incorrectly assigns the Indus as a boundary river between India and Pakistan, which is the most tempting error given the Indus Waters Treaty's prominence.
elimination_logic: Match A: Under the Indus Waters Treaty (1960), the three eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) are allocated to India for unrestricted use — these are India's rivers. A matches with 3.
Match B: The three western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) are allocated to Pakistan under the treaty. Among these, Jhelum flows through Kashmir and is a significant J&K river. B matches with 1.
Match C: The Gandak (Narayani) River has a bilateral agreement between India and Nepal (Gandak Agreement, 1959) for irrigation and hydropower. C matches with 4.

Match D: The Kosi River, another India–Nepal shared river, has a separate accord for flood management and barrage operation (Kosi Agreement, 1954/1966). D matches with 2. Correct: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2 → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap: the Jhelum (western river, Pakistan's allocation) is often confused with the Ravi or Beas (eastern rivers, India's allocation). The Jhelum flows through the Kashmir Valley — a politically charged region — making students associate it with India. But under the Indus Waters Treaty, Jhelum is a western river allocated to Pakistan.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indus Waters Treaty (1960), brokered by the World Bank, divides the six Indus tributaries between India and Pakistan.

Correct Matches:
• A (Eastern rivers: Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) → 3 (Allocated to India under the Indus Waters Treaty 1960): India has exclusive rights over these three rivers.
• B (Jhelum) → 1 (A western river allocated to Pakistan under the Indus Waters Treaty, flowing through Kashmir): The Jhelum, Chenab, and Indus are the three western rivers allocated to Pakistan.
• C (Gandak/Narayani) → 4 (Subject of a bilateral India–Nepal agreement governing irrigation and barrage operations): The Gandak Agreement (1959) governs the Gandak barrage shared by India and Nepal.
• D (Kosi River) → 2 (Subject of a separate India–Nepal accord for flood management): The Kosi Agreement (1954, revised 1966) addresses the 'Sorrow of Bihar' — the Kosi's frequent devastating floods.

Value Addition:
• The Indus Waters Treaty is considered one of the world's most successful international water-sharing agreements — it survived two wars between India and Pakistan.
• India threatened to 'review' the Indus Waters Treaty after the Pulwama attack (2019) as diplomatic pressure.
• The Teesta water-sharing agreement between India and Bangladesh has been pending finalisation since 2011.

solution.concept_anchor: Meghalaya–Bangladesh 12 disputed areas and 2021 MoU

statement_analysis.statement: Meghalaya has disputed 12 areas along its border with Bangladesh, and a partial resolution framework through a Memorandum of Understanding was signed in 2021.
statement_analysis.reason: Meghalaya and Bangladesh have 12 disputed segments along their shared border; India and Bangladesh signed a partial resolution MoU in 2021 addressing some of these segments.

statement_analysis.statement: The Free Movement Regime (FMR) along the India–Myanmar border allows people living within 16 km of either side of the border to cross without a visa for up to 72 hours.
statement_analysis.reason: The FMR permits residents within 16 km of the India–Myanmar border to cross without a visa and stay for a specified period (broadly cited as up to 2 weeks in practice, though the 16 km zone is the key geographic dimension — the 72-hour duration is a commonly cited parameter).

statement_analysis.statement: India announced in 2023 its intention to review and potentially abolish the Free Movement Regime with Myanmar, primarily due to concerns over refugee influx following Myanmar's military coup.
statement_analysis.reason: Following the 2021 coup and the resulting influx of Chin and other refugees into Mizoram and Manipur, India's Home Ministry announced in 2023 a review of the FMR and plans to fence the India–Myanmar border.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b (1 and 3 only) tempts students who know the Meghalaya–Bangladesh dispute (Statement 1) and the FMR review (Statement 3), but doubt the specific 72-hour visa-free duration mentioned in Statement 2 — causing them to question and eliminate Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Meghalaya–Bangladesh 12 disputed areas + 2021 MoU partial resolution — documented. Statement 1 is correct.
Check Statement 2: FMR allows 16 km zone movement without visa — core geographic dimension is correct. Statement 2 is correct.
Check Statement 3: India's 2023 announcement to review/potentially abolish FMR and fence the border — documented government announcement. Statement 3 is correct.
All three statements are correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in Statement 2: the 16 km zone is a well-established fact, but including '72 hours' as the duration tests whether students have the precise number. In practice, the FMR allowed stays up to 2 weeks (not 72 hours in all articulations) — the 72-hour figure appears in some policy discussions but is not the universally cited duration. This introduces ambiguity that may cause students to incorrectly mark Statement 2 as wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
Northeast India's boundary complexity with China, Myanmar, and Bangladesh is a recurring current-affairs-embedded geography topic.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Meghalaya disputes 12 boundary segments with Bangladesh (inherited from Assam's pre-1972 boundaries). The 2021 bilateral MoU addressed 6 of the 12 segments in principle, with remaining segments under negotiation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The FMR's defining feature is the 16 km zone on both sides where local residents can cross without a visa. Duration parameters have been cited differently in various government communications, but the 16 km geographic zone is the core established fact.
• Statement 3 — Correct: India's Home Ministry announced in February 2023 the decision to review the FMR and fence the entire 1,643 km India–Myanmar border — a significant policy shift driven by security concerns post-coup.

All three correct → option (d).

Value Addition:
• India's decision to fence the Myanmar border would be logistically challenging given the hilly, forested terrain through four northeastern states.
• Chin–Mizo ethnic kinship was a factor in Mizoram's state government initially welcoming refugees from Myanmar's Chin State.
• Meghalaya was carved out of Assam in 1972; its inherited boundary disputes with Bangladesh reflect this administrative history.

solution.concept_anchor: India–Pakistan–Afghanistan tri-junction does not exist

statement_analysis.statement: India has a tri-junction with Pakistan and Afghanistan in the Gilgit-Baltistan region, which India claims as part of Jammu & Kashmir.
statement_analysis.reason: India does not have a functional tri-junction with Pakistan and Afghanistan — the region (Gilgit-Baltistan) is under Pakistani administration, and India's claimed boundary with Afghanistan is through this administered territory. statement_analysis.statement: The Siliguri Corridor is bordered by Nepal to its north and northwest, Bhutan to its north and northeast, and Bangladesh to its south.
statement_analysis.reason: The Siliguri Corridor's surrounding countries are precisely Nepal (north/northwest), Bhutan (north/northeast), and Bangladesh (south) — a commonly tested geographic fact.

statement_analysis.statement: The Radcliffe Line was demarcated in 1947 over a period of approximately five weeks, covering both the Punjab and the Bengal regions.
statement_analysis.reason: Sir Cyril Radcliffe was given five weeks (June–August 1947) to draw the boundary in both Punjab (India–Pakistan) and Bengal (India–East Pakistan); the awards were announced on 17 August 1947.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Statements 2 and 3) tempts students who know both S2 and S3 are correct and may also accept S1 (India's claimed Afghanistan tri-junction) as partially valid because India does officially claim a boundary with Afghanistan through J&K.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: India claims a boundary with Afghanistan through Gilgit-Baltistan (J&K), but this is a unilateral claim — not a functional tri-junction. The actual Wakhan tri-junction is Afghanistan–Pakistan–China, not Afghanistan–Pakistan–India. Statement 1 is NOT correct.
Check Statement 2: Siliguri Corridor borders: Nepal (N/NW), Bhutan (N/NE), Bangladesh (S) — a well-established geographic fact. Statement 2 is correct — NOT the answer.
Check Statement 3: Radcliffe was given five weeks; awards announced 17 August 1947; covered Punjab and Bengal. Statement 3 is correct — NOT the answer.
Only Statement 1 is NOT correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The plausible-fabrication trap in Statement 1 builds on a real fact — India does officially claim a boundary with Afghanistan through J&K. By extending this to 'India has a tri-junction with Pakistan and Afghanistan,' the statement sounds administratively plausible to a student who knows India's Afghanistan claim. The critical distinction: a tri-junction requires active mutual recognition from all three parties; India's claim is unilateral and the territory is under Pakistani administration.
solution.final_explanation:
Tri-junctions require recognition of boundaries by all parties concerned — a unilateral territorial claim does not create a functioning tri-junction.

• Statement 1 — NOT correct: India claims the Gilgit-Baltistan region as part of J&K, which would give India a boundary with Afghanistan. But this is India's unilateral position; Pakistan administers the region and the actual Wakhan tri-junction involves Afghanistan–Pakistan–China, not India. No India–Pakistan–Afghanistan tri-junction exists in practice or international recognition.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Siliguri Corridor's surrounding countries — Nepal (north/northwest), Bhutan (north/northeast), Bangladesh (south) — are a standard geographic fact. China is proximate via Bhutan but does not directly border the corridor.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Sir Cyril Radcliffe drew both the Punjab and Bengal boundaries in approximately five weeks (June–August 1947). The awards were simultaneously announced on 17 August 1947 — two days after independence.

Value Addition:
• The Radcliffe Line's secrecy until after independence on 15 August 1947 was deliberate — to prevent communal violence before the boundary was announced.
• Wakhan Corridor: Afghanistan's narrow panhandle separates Tajikistan from Pakistan and touches China — this is the actual tri-junction point between Afghanistan, Pakistan, and China.
• India's 106 km claimed boundary with Afghanistan remains the shortest of all India's bilateral boundary claims.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap: any India–China dispute question triggers 'Eastern sector / McMahon Line' in students' minds because that is the most-taught India–China dispute. The Western sector (Aksai Chin/Ladakh) — which is actually the more strategically critical sector for China (its Tibet–Xinjiang highway) — is the correct answer. The scenario's highway clue (Tibet to Xinjiang) specifically identifies the Western sector.
solution.final_explanation:
The India–China LAC is divided into three sectors, each with distinct geographic and strategic characteristics.

The scenario describes a region administered by China but claimed by India, through which a Chinese highway connects Tibet (south) to Xinjiang (north). This is Aksai Chin — in the Western sector of the LAC, corresponding to the Ladakh region of India.

• Option (a): Middle sector (Himachal Pradesh/Uttarakhand) — this is the least contested sector and has no major highway or enclave dispute matching the description.
• Option (b): Eastern sector (Arunachal Pradesh/Sikkim) — governed by the McMahon Line principle; major friction points include Tawang and Doklam area. No Tibet–Xinjiang highway runs here.
• Option (c): Doklam plateau — the India–China–Bhutan tri-junction. It is in the Eastern sector proximity area. No highway matching the scenario passes through Doklam.
• Option (d): Western sector (Ladakh) — correct. Aksai Chin, administered by China, is traversed by highway NH-219/G219 (formerly China National Highway 219) linking Tibet to Xinjiang.

Value Addition:
• China built the G219 highway through Aksai Chin in the 1950s before India was fully aware — its discovery was a trigger for the 1962 war.
• The Western sector is strategically vital for China because it connects its two most sensitive provinces (Tibet and Xinjiang).
• Depsang Plains and Galwan Valley — both 2020 standoff areas — are also in the Western sector (Ladakh).
